what: One YAML format and CLI to run training tasks on GPU clouds, Kubernetes and own machines (SSH fleets), through a self-hosted server.
problem_here: Goal 3: the kit has no way to start, watch, stop and clean up a run on a rented GPU. The alternative is one hand-written adapter per provider.
mechanism: Harness writes a task file and calls the CLI. Settings cover spot_policy, retry on no-capacity, interruption and error, max_price per hour, max_duration, stop_duration, idle_duration, utilization_policy and tags; status comes from dstack run get --json.
evidence: Vendor docs and release notes read 2026-11-11: https://dstack.ai/docs/reference/dstack.yml/task/ ; https://github.com/dstackai/dstack/releases/tag/0.22.6 ; https://github.com/dstackai/dstack/releases/tag/0.22.7 . Feature claims are the vendor's own; no independent measurement found.
maturity: Repository created 2022-01-04; 0.22.7 released 2026-11-04, about weekly releases; MPL-2.0; 2,310 stars in the sweep (weak signal).
cost: Server process and its state (WSL2 on Windows, not native); Docker images; cloud credentials held by the server; admin token printed at start; no total-spend cap; max_duration off by default; retry can multiply spend; orphan cleanup is report-only by default and skips volumes; vendor agent skill is extra attack surface; weekly release churn.
simpler_alternative: Plain SSH to one rented machine, the kit's own expctl on it, and a remote autostop script.
reason: Best feature match found for preemption retry, per-hour price ceiling, time cap and idle teardown, with an active release cadence. The trial must show how it behaves when the server dies and that harness-written limits hold.
cheap_local_trial: In WSL2 with systemd, Docker and NVIDIA Container Toolkit: install a pinned version in a venv, start the server, register the WSL2 host as an SSH fleet, run a 2-minute task with max_duration, retry and utilization_policy set, then kill the server mid-run and record what keeps running. No cloud account or money. Not checked: whether an SSH fleet may point at the same host. About 30 minutes, not 5.

what: Python library that aggregates GPU offers and prices from 18 providers into offline, versioned catalogs that can be queried by memory, GPU count, price ceiling and spot.
problem_here: A pre-launch cost bound needs a price per hour; the kit has no price source.
mechanism: gpuhunt.query(min_memory=..., min_gpu_count=..., max_price=..., spot=...) over downloaded catalog files.
evidence: Repository README read 2026-11-11: https://github.com/dstackai/gpuhunt . Maintainer description only; nobody measured catalog accuracy.
maturity: First release not seen; 0.1.35 is the version named in the dstack 0.22.6 notes (2026-10-29), its own release date not seen; MPL-2.0; 59 stars, 293 commits (weak signal).
cost: One package plus its dependencies; catalog can be stale; list price is not the billed price; network needed to refresh.
simpler_alternative: The user types the hourly price ceiling into the kit config; the provider's own offer listing gives the price at launch.
reason: Useful only if the remote module supports several providers; a user-entered price ceiling is enough for one.
cheap_local_trial: In a throwaway WSL2 venv install the pinned version, run one query for a 24 GB GPU under a price ceiling and compare three offers with the providers' own pricing pages. About 10 minutes; needs network; whether an account is needed was not checked.

what: Launches clusters and managed jobs on many clouds and Kubernetes, with spot recovery and autostop.
problem_here: Same gap as dstack: remote launch, recovery and teardown.
mechanism: Managed jobs relaunch after preemption; autostop and autodown run on the remote cluster, so they work with the local machine off; max_restarts_on_errors bounds restarts.
evidence: Vendor docs read 2026-11-11: https://docs.skypilot.ai/en/latest/examples/managed-jobs.html ; https://docs.skypilot.ai/en/latest/reference/auto-stop.html ; release page https://github.com/skypilot-org/skypilot/releases/tag/v0.14.2 . Vendor description; no independent measurement read.
maturity: First release 2022 (from memory, not re-checked); v0.14.2 released 2026-10-28; Apache-2.0 (from memory, not re-checked); adoption signal not collected because it was not in the sweep.
cost: Package with many cloud SDKs; API server and jobs controller (a dedicated controller machine costs about 0.25 USD per hour per the docs); a recovered job restarts from scratch unless the code checkpoints; no cost limit or budget feature on the pages read; cloud credentials on the launching machine.
simpler_alternative: SSH plus a remote autostop script; or dstack if a control plane is wanted.
reason: Credible second backend and the source of the remote-side autostop design, but it was read only as the alternative to dstack. Compare the two in one trial before choosing.
cheap_local_trial: In a WSL2 venv install the pinned version, run its credential check and a dry-run launch and read the plan and price it prints. A real launch needs a cloud credential or a local Kubernetes cluster. Command names are from memory, not re-checked.

candidate: Modal (serverless GPU platform; docs as read 2026-11-11, no version number)
what: Runs Python functions on GPUs billed by use, with volumes for checkpoints.
problem_here: A low-ceremony way to run short training or evaluation jobs remotely without managing machines.
mechanism: Function timeout (default 300 s, maximum 24 h), retries (maximum 10), volumes for checkpoints, detached runs that survive client disconnect.
evidence: Vendor docs read 2026-11-11: https://modal.com/docs/guide/preemption ; https://modal.com/docs/guide/timeouts ; https://modal.com/docs/examples/long-training . One outside cost report, measured by a paper's authors: 200 evaluation rollouts for 3.49 USD on eight L4 shards, https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07441 (2026-11-05).
maturity: First release not checked; proprietary hosted service; client license not checked; several sweep repositories use it (weak signal).
cost: Account and money; GPU functions are always preemptible; the 24 h ceiling forces checkpoint and retry chains; the training command must be wrapped as a platform function; service credentials on the local machine; code and data leave the machine.
simpler_alternative: A rented machine over SSH, which runs the unmodified training command.
reason: Good fit for sharded evaluation and short runs; poor fit for the kit's uniform run contract because the training command must be rewritten as a platform function.
cheap_local_trial: none without an account. With the owner's own account: a 5-minute GPU function with timeout and retries set that writes a checkpoint to a volume; kill the local client and confirm what continues.

candidate: Prepaid-credit provider account as the outer spend cap (billing rules of Vast.ai and RunPod as read 2026-11-11)
what: Use a provider that bills against a prepaid balance, load only the budget and keep auto-recharge off, so the balance is a hard ceiling outside the kit.
problem_here: Brief: never spend without a user-set cap. The orchestrators read cap price per hour, not total spend, and hyperscaler budget alerts lag.
mechanism: When the balance reaches zero the provider stops the instances; the kit's own ledger is the inner cap.
evidence: Vendor billing docs read 2026-11-11: https://docs.vast.ai/guides/reference/billing.md ; https://docs.runpod.io/get-started/billing-information ; https://docs.runpod.io/pods/pricing . Vendor statements of policy, not measurements.
maturity: Standing billing model at both providers; policies can change without notice; not a software release.
cost: At zero balance work can be lost: one provider terminates pods that have no network volume, the other deletes data after a grace period unless a card is saved. Storage keeps billing while stopped. Credits are non-refundable at one provider. One provider's default spend limit is 80 USD per hour, far above a small budget.
simpler_alternative: Hyperscaler budget alerts, which are delayed and do not stop spending by default.
reason: The only hard total cap found in this sweep. It works by stopping machines, so it must be paired with off-host checkpoints.
cheap_local_trial: none locally. With the owner's own account: load a small balance with auto-recharge off, start the cheapest instance and watch what happens as the balance runs down.

candidate: Kit-owned budget ledger with a worst-case cost bound checked before every launch
what: A stdlib ledger of runs, wall time, GPU-hours, money and agent tokens. A launch is refused when price per hour times maximum duration times allowed retries would exceed what is left.
problem_here: Goals 1 and 3: limits must be enforced by harness code. Neither orchestrator read has a total-spend cap, and dstack max_duration defaults to off.
mechanism: Limits live in one config file; expctl computes the bound, writes the duration limit and price ceiling into the remote job, and debits actual use after the run.
evidence: Absence of a total cap in vendor docs read 2026-11-11: https://dstack.ai/docs/reference/dstack.yml/task/ ; https://docs.skypilot.ai/en/latest/examples/managed-jobs.html . Industry report of about 2,000 USD lost to one duplicate execution, authors' own account: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06890 (2026-09-24).
maturity: Design pattern, no release; the same idea as queue admission control.
cost: Small stdlib code; needs a price input; the bill can differ from the bound (storage, data transfer, minimum billing units), so the bound needs a margin.
simpler_alternative: Trust the orchestrator's per-hour price ceiling and a wall-clock timeout.
reason: The brief requires a user-set cap and no tool read provides one. The same ledger bounds the unattended loop locally.
cheap_local_trial: Unit test with fake CPU runs and a fake hourly price: assert the launch that would cross the cap is refused and that the ledger survives a crash between debit and launch. Minutes.

what: A watchdog started on the rented machine that shuts it down at a hard deadline, when the run ends, or when GPU use or the heartbeat stays idle, without needing the local machine.
problem_here: Brief quality attribute 3: no job left billing after 12 unattended hours, even if the agent session or the local machine dies.
mechanism: Deadline and idle threshold are written at launch; the check runs on the remote host; the final action is stop or delete.
evidence: SkyPilot docs state the autostop check runs on the remote cluster so the local machine can be off: https://docs.skypilot.ai/en/latest/reference/auto-stop.html . dstack has idle_duration and utilization_policy: https://dstack.ai/docs/reference/dstack.yml/task/ . Both read 2026-11-11; vendor descriptions.
maturity: Shipped feature in both orchestrators; the pattern is older than either.
cost: A stopped machine can still bill for disk; self-delete needs provider rights on the host, which trades against credential exposure; too short an idle window kills data-loading phases.
simpler_alternative: A local watcher that calls the provider API, which fails when the local machine is off.
reason: The only teardown path that survives loss of the control plane. Both orchestrators implement it, which is the evidence that it is needed.
cheap_local_trial: In WSL2 start a fake run with a watchdog that ends the run and writes a marker when the heartbeat file is older than N seconds or a deadline passes; kill the controller and check the marker appears. Minutes.

what: Every remote resource the kit creates carries the run ID as a tag or name. A separate reconcile command lists resources by tag, compares them with the run records and reports or deletes leftovers.
problem_here: Brief: always clean up what it started. A crash between create and record leaves a billing resource nobody tracks.
mechanism: Write intent to the run record before the create call; tag at creation; reconcile at every session start and at loop end; report by default, delete only resources carrying the kit's own tag.
evidence: dstack 0.22.6 release notes (2026-10-29) add this because a server bug or crash can leave resources orphaned; report-only by default; volumes and gateways not covered: https://github.com/dstackai/dstack/releases/tag/0.22.6 . Read 2026-11-11; the vendor's own statement.
maturity: Shipped in dstack since 0.22.6 for five backends; Kubernetes added in 0.22.7 (2026-11-04).
cost: Needs list and delete rights on the account; a wrong tag filter could delete other people's resources, so it must match only the kit's tags; volumes and snapshots are easy to miss.
simpler_alternative: Rely on the orchestrator's own cleanup and on the provider console.
reason: Vendor release notes confirm the failure is real. The brief's shared-account users require that only tagged resources are touched.
cheap_local_trial: A fake provider as a JSON file of instances with tags; kill the launcher between create and record; assert reconcile reports exactly the leftover and ignores untagged entries. Minutes.

candidate: Periodic atomic checkpoint to off-host storage plus verified resume, as the only preemption contract
what: Training saves complete checkpoints on a timer to storage that outlives the machine. A preempted run resumes from the last complete one and the harness verifies that the step counter and metrics continue.
problem_here: Brief: survive preemption. The kit has graceful stop and resume locally; remote preemption may give no warning at all.
mechanism: Write to a temporary name then rename; sync to a bucket or volume; resume reads the newest complete checkpoint; never rely on a termination signal arriving.
evidence: Provider docs read 2026-11-11: AWS two minutes, best effort, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/spot-instance-termination-notices.html ; GCP no notice by default and up to 30 s shutdown, https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/spot ; Azure 30 s, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/spot-vms ; restart from scratch unless the user checkpoints, https://docs.skypilot.ai/en/latest/examples/managed-jobs.html . Restart alone took 127 s on 32 GPUs, authors' measurement, https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22014 .
maturity: Standard practice; documented by every provider read.
cost: Checkpoint time and storage cost; storage credentials on the rented host; resume must restore optimizer, scheduler, data position and random state or results change.
simpler_alternative: Catch the termination signal and save once, which fails where notice is zero or shorter than the save.
reason: Notice ranges from none to two minutes and is best effort everywhere, so signal handling cannot be the contract.
cheap_local_trial: A fake training loop on the local GPU; hard-kill it at 20 random moments; assert each resume loads a complete checkpoint and the loss curve continues without a jump. Minutes.

what: A small poller on the rented machine that watches the provider's metadata endpoint and triggers one extra checkpoint when a termination notice appears.
problem_here: Reduces work lost between periodic checkpoints on providers that give notice.
mechanism: AWS: poll the instance-action metadata path about every 5 s. GCP: the preempted metadata value. Azure: Scheduled Events.
evidence: Provider docs read 2026-11-11: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/spot-instance-termination-notices.html ; https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/spot ; https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/spot-vms . No measurement of how often the notice arrives in time was found.
maturity: Documented provider features of long standing.
cost: One code path per provider; notice is best effort; a save can take longer than the notice; no such signal is documented at the marketplace and serverless providers read.
simpler_alternative: A shorter periodic checkpoint interval.
reason: An optimisation on top of periodic checkpoints; worth building only if measured lost work is large.
cheap_local_trial: none against real endpoints. Simulate: send the termination signal to a fake run and measure time to a complete checkpoint against 30 s and 120 s budgets.

what: Checkpoint interval near the square root of 2 times checkpoint cost times mean time between interruptions.
problem_here: The kit has no stated basis for choosing a checkpoint interval on interruptible machines.
mechanism: One line of arithmetic from measured checkpoint seconds and an assumed interruption rate.
evidence: Seen only in search summaries on 2026-11-11 (a classic high-performance-computing result, for example arXiv 1310.8456); primary sources not opened. Unverified in this note.
maturity: Decades-old result (from memory).
cost: Needs an interruption-rate estimate the user rarely has; assumes independent failures.
simpler_alternative: A fixed interval such as every 15 to 30 minutes.
reason: Cheap to add as dated advice in the resume reference, but the primary source was not read here and its main input is usually a guess.
cheap_local_trial: Python prompt: a 60 s checkpoint and one interruption per 4 h give about 22 minutes; compare with the interval in use.

candidate: Guard coverage for provisioning commands, vendor agent skills and paid MCP tools
what: The PreToolUse guard treats cloud provisioning and rental commands, skill installers and money-spending MCP tools as ask (deny when nobody can answer) unless they come from the kit's own budgeted launcher.
problem_here: Vendor flows assume a person confirms spending. In unattended mode nobody does, and the agent can call a vendor CLI directly and bypass the ledger.
mechanism: Pattern rules for apply, launch, create and similar verbs of known CLIs, for skill-install commands, and for MCP tools named like submit, create, deploy or run; the kit's launcher is the single allowed spend path.
evidence: Vendor skill that asks the agent to get user confirmation before apply and to request permissions outside the sandbox: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dstackai/dstack/master/skills/dstack/SKILL.md . MCP server with paid tools and no stated limit: https://github.com/runcomfy-com/runcomfy-mcp . CLI that can store its key in a project-local file: https://github.com/jyswee/computegpu-cli . All read 2026-11-11.
maturity: Extends the kit's existing guard (38 tested decisions per README.md).
cost: Pattern lists go stale as CLIs change; a pattern guard cannot see calls made from inside scripts; extra asks in attended use.
simpler_alternative: Advice in the skill text only.
reason: The kit already gates one vendor's paid tools this way. This closes the same hole for the remote module and keeps the ledger the only spend path.
cheap_local_trial: Add the patterns to a copy of the guard config and run the guard tests with ten new command strings; assert ask in default mode and deny in bypass mode. Minutes.

what: Command-line wrapper that runs a training command, guarantees a log, classifies the failure and emails the result.
problem_here: none found for the package: the kit already wraps runs, so it would duplicate expctl.
mechanism: Process-boundary wrapper; 15 ordered regular-expression rules; email notification with attachments.
evidence: Preprint, not peer reviewed (2026-07-01): https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01409 . Package index: https://pypi.org/project/gpualert/ . Read 2026-11-11. All results measured by the tool's author.
maturity: 0.1.0 on 2026-05-26; 0.1.6 on 2026-10-27; MIT; single author; 1 upvote in the sweep (no adoption signal).
cost: Python 3.10 or newer; six dependencies; Linux and macOS only; needs an SMTP account and a stored mail credential; overlaps expctl.
simpler_alternative: Port the four ideas into expctl and runlog (next line).
reason: Breaks the stdlib-only and native-Windows constraints and duplicates the run controller. Its ideas are worth taking; the dependency is not.
cheap_local_trial: none on native Windows. In WSL2 it could wrap a failing script, but notification needs mail credentials; not recommended.

candidate: Ordered-rule failure classifier, log created before launch, notifier isolation, named skipped artifacts (ideas from GPUAlert 0.1.6)
what: Four small properties of a run wrapper: classify the failure by first-match-wins rules from specific to generic, with a fix hint; create the log file before the child starts; never let a notification error change the run's exit status; list by name anything left out of a report.
problem_here: expctl reports crash, NaN, stall, lost and timeout states but not the cause. An unattended loop needs the cause to choose between retry, smaller batch and stop, and a remote run that fails before its first line must still leave a log.
mechanism: Stdlib regular expressions in a fixed order (out of memory before generic runtime error before bare traceback); the parent opens the log; notifier calls sit inside a catch-all; skipped files are reported.
evidence: Author-measured, preprint (2026-07-01): macro-F1 0.997 for ordered rules against 0.830 for the same patterns unordered and 0.133 for exit-code inspection, on 12 hardware-reproduced classes; log present in 20 of 20 exec-failure trials against 0 of 20 for shell redirection; exit status unchanged in 15 of 15 notifier failures; overhead about 3 ms. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01409 . Read 2026-11-11. One GPU model, PyTorch only, 3 of 15 classes synthetic, 24 real-world logs.
maturity: Idea level; reference implementation MIT, 0.1.6 on 2026-10-27.
cost: The rule list needs upkeep as framework messages change; unknown errors fall to the generic rule; a classification can be wrong and must be shown as a hint.
simpler_alternative: Keep the current five states and let the analyst subagent read the log.
reason: Stdlib-only, tiny, and needed by both the unattended loop and the remote module. The evidence is one author's own test, so adopt the mechanism and verify it on the kit's own logs.
cheap_local_trial: Write the ordered rules as one stdlib function; run it on logs from the kit's fake crash, NaN and out-of-memory runs plus a forced exec failure; compare with unordered matching. Under an hour.

candidate: gpualert-eval labelled failure-log corpus (repository at 12 commits)
what: 474 training-failure logs labelled in 15 classes, with fault-injection scripts and baselines.
problem_here: The kit has no labelled logs to test a failure classifier against.
mechanism: Read corpus/labels.jsonl and the log files as text; score the kit's classifier.
evidence: Repository read 2026-11-11: https://github.com/Parv-01/gpualert-eval . Composition per the paper https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01409 : 360 logs from one V100, 90 synthetic, 24 from public issue trackers.
maturity: 12 commits, 0 stars, MIT; single author; no release tag seen.
cost: A download of third-party files, to be done by the owner and pinned to a commit; logs come from one GPU model and one framework; log text may address a reader and must be treated as data.
simpler_alternative: Generate the kit's own failure logs from its fake runs.
reason: The cheapest available yardstick for the classifier; development-time only, never shipped with the kit.
cheap_local_trial: The owner fetches the repository at a pinned commit into an empty folder and runs the kit's classifier over the text files; nothing from the repository is executed. Minutes.

what: Before a real launch, and always before a paid one, run the exact command for a few steps at the largest batch and sequence length and check memory fit, data access, checkpoint write and the evaluation call.
problem_here: Failed launches waste budget and, remotely, money. The unattended loop will propose many configurations.
mechanism: A preflight option on expctl launch: a short run locally or on the target, peak GPU memory read, refusal on failure, result stored in the run record.
evidence: 30,920 fine-tuning experiments: 63% gave no valid run, 9,144 rejected before launch and 10,395 failed at run time, measured by the paper's authors (workshop paper, 2026-10-29): https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40983 . GPU out of memory was 18% of dead-lettered jobs in an industry report: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06890 . Read 2026-11-11. Caveat: the failure share is high partly because the sweep was built to probe limits.
maturity: Common practice; the paper calls it admission control.
cost: About a minute per configuration; a short run misses failures that appear late (fragmentation, evaluation-time memory, long sequences in later batches).
simpler_alternative: Launch and let the crash state report it.
reason: Stdlib-only, protects budget locally and remotely, and has the largest measured base rate behind it of anything in this sweep.
cheap_local_trial: On the 32 GB GPU run a training command for two steps at its largest batch, read peak memory from the GPU vendor's query tool and compare with a full run's peak. Minutes.

what: Per-experiment records of LLM fine-tuning runs: validity flag, peak GPU memory and tokens per second, across 33 models, 4 GPU types and 1 to 32 GPUs.
problem_here: Could seed a memory-fit and throughput estimate for preflight without running anything.
mechanism: Look up the nearest model size, GPU type and batch size; read validity and memory.
evidence: Dataset card read 2026-11-11: https://huggingface.co/datasets/ibm-research/LLMFineTuningBench . Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40983 (2026-10-29). Measured by the authors on their own cluster.
maturity: Released with the paper in October 2026; Apache-2.0; no adoption signal yet.
cost: A download; GPU types and software differ from the user's; an estimate from other hardware can be wrong in both directions.
simpler_alternative: Measure on the user's own GPU with the preflight run.
reason: A measured preflight is more reliable than a lookup. The data may still give the fine-tuning reference dated rules of thumb.
cheap_local_trial: The owner downloads the table and tabulates failure share by batch size and model size for the GPU class nearest their own. About 15 minutes.

candidate: Single-writer launch lock, idempotent launch key and one shared limits file
what: Only one process may admit launches at a time; each launch has a key derived from run name and config hash so a retry cannot start a second copy; every limit is read from one file by both the loop and the launcher.
problem_here: An unattended loop with retries, a resumed session or two agent sessions can launch the same paid job twice.
mechanism: Exclusive-create lock file; launch key recorded before the provider call; timeouts derived from the configured maximum run time.
evidence: Industry experience report over more than 40,000 training jobs, authors' own account (2026-09-24): a queue timeout shorter than the job caused duplicate execution costing about 2,000 USD; a race started 4 GPU tasks on a 2-instance cluster; fixes were a single dispatcher, a timeout near 1.5 times the longest job, and limits bound to one shared variable. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06890 . Read 2026-11-11. One organisation.
maturity: Standard distributed-systems practice.
cost: A stale lock after a crash needs a safe takeover rule; lock files behave differently on network drives.
simpler_alternative: Trust the agent not to launch twice.
reason: Stdlib-only, and it protects running jobs and budgets, which the brief ranks above features.
cheap_local_trial: Two shells start the same launch at once; assert exactly one run starts on NTFS and under WSL2; kill the holder and assert takeover after the timeout. Minutes.

what: Changes the number of GPUs of a running distributed training job without stopping it.
problem_here: none found for single-node training. It does show that restart cost can exceed a two-minute notice.
mechanism: Live reconfiguration of parallel groups inside the training framework.
evidence: Authors' measurement (2026-05-21): 14 to 23 times faster than checkpoint and restart; restart baseline 127.1 s on 32 GPUs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22014 . Read 2026-11-11, page partly read; baselines partly modelled.
maturity: Preprint; no code released; needs a fast cluster interconnect.
cost: Not usable without the authors' system.
simpler_alternative: Checkpoint and restart.
reason: Multi-node only, no code, and the brief says single-node is the common case.
cheap_local_trial: none

candidate: Candidate ledger, selection-invariance selftest and full trace retention
what: Record every candidate the loop tries, not only the kept ones; test that the keep decision is unchanged when test-set results are replaced or inverted; keep logs and code for each candidate so a reviewer can audit.
problem_here: Brief quality attribute 1: no kept result may depend on leakage or a lucky pick, and a reviewer must be able to verify each from saved artifacts.
mechanism: Append-only ledger written by harness code; a selftest that reruns the keep rule with test scores negated; per-candidate snapshots.
evidence: Study of autonomous research systems, measured by its authors (arXiv 2509.08713 v2, read 2026-11-11; the 2026-10-05 journal article with the same title returned 403 and was not read): the top candidate was chosen 78.5% of the time with real test results and 43.5% with inverted ones in one system, 82.0% and 31.5% in another; an auditor reached 55% accuracy from the paper alone and 82% with logs and code. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.08713
maturity: Method described in one paper; the ledger itself is ordinary experiment tracking.
cost: Disk for traces; the selftest needs a path that feeds fake test scores without touching the sealed set.
simpler_alternative: Keep only the journal entries the agent writes.
reason: Direct measured evidence that agents select on test results when they can, and that logs plus code cut audit errors by more than half.
cheap_local_trial: Ten fake candidates with validation scores and fake test scores; rerun the keep rule with the test scores negated; assert the kept set is identical. Minutes, no GPU.

candidate: Hidden verifier, tripwires, repeated-call detection and token caps for the unattended loop
what: Keep the evaluator out of the agent's reach, plant canaries that halt the loop when touched, stop after N identical consecutive tool calls, and cap agent tokens per run and per loop.
problem_here: Goal 1 and the ports: the loop must hold with agents that try shortcuts more often than the one the kit was built on.
mechanism: Sealed evaluator invoked by harness code; canary files in sealed paths; a counter in the hook; a token budget in the ledger.
evidence: Benchmark paper, authors' measurement over 1,300 rollouts (2026-06-05): reward-hacking attempts in 13.8% of rollouts and shipped exploits in 10.2%, none successful against hidden verifiers; exploit rates of 26.0%, 22.0% and 0.5% for three agent models; up to 877 identical consecutive tool calls; tokens per trial median 7.6 million, maximum 877.4 million. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07682 . Read 2026-11-11; page truncated, appendix not read.
maturity: Protections are described in the paper, not released as a library.
cost: Canaries can trip on honest reads by tools; the three agent products do not expose token counts the same way.
simpler_alternative: Rely on the existing sealed and frozen path rules.
reason: Rates differ about fifty-fold between agent models, so protections tuned on one agent cannot be assumed to hold on the other two.
cheap_local_trial: A scripted fake agent that reads a canary and repeats one tool call 20 times; assert the loop halts on each with a clear record. Minutes.

what: The frozen evaluator must give chance-level scores or an error on known-bad outputs (empty, constant, shuffled labels) and must check structure strictly, not by keyword.
problem_here: A frozen evaluator that is lenient freezes the leniency in; the loop then optimises toward whatever it lets through.
mechanism: A selftest runs the evaluator on negative controls before the loop starts and whenever the evaluator hash changes.
evidence: Preprint (October 2026), authors' measurement, single seed: a keyword scorer gave 0.660 and 0.650 to two models while a strict structural check gave 6 of 6 and 0. https://huggingface.co/papers/2610.02142 . Read 2026-11-11, page partly read.
maturity: Negative controls are standard in experimental science; one small paper as ML evidence here.
cost: The user must define what a known-bad output is for the task.
simpler_alternative: Trust the user's evaluator as given.
reason: Cheap, stdlib-only, and it guards the one component the whole loop trusts.
cheap_local_trial: Feed the evaluator an empty prediction file, a constant one and one with shuffled labels; assert each scores at chance or raises. Minutes.

what: A mechanical check that the checkpoint used for the final evaluation was selected on validation data only.
problem_here: The kit seals the test set against reads by the agent, but the user's training code can still pick its best checkpoint by test score.
mechanism: Selection reads only validation metric keys from the run record; the final evaluation runs once on the selected checkpoint; the run record stores which split drove selection.
evidence: Preprint (2026-07-28), the authors' own correction: apparent gains were an artifact of selecting checkpoints on small test splits (differences up to 0.05 in recall at 5); with validation selection the result was 0.673 plus or minus 0.019. https://huggingface.co/papers/2607.25572 . Read 2026-11-11.
maturity: Textbook practice; one recent worked example.
cost: Needs the user's metrics to be named by split.
simpler_alternative: State the rule in the validity reference only.
reason: A small extension of the existing metric-selection config; the failure it prevents is the brief's first quality attribute.
cheap_local_trial: Unit test: a run record with validation and test keys; assert the selector ignores test keys and that the final evaluation refuses to run twice. Minutes.

what: When a language model is pretrained for many passes over limited data, validation loss is U-shaped in batch size with the best value near 64 sequences; repacking sequences each epoch beats reshuffling; weight tying plus weight decay on embeddings helps.
problem_here: Goal 5: small-data language-model pretraining on one GPU is a common case, and this is recent evidence on batch size for it.
mechanism: A smaller batch gives more updates and more implicit regularisation per unit of compute.
evidence: Authors' measurement on 153M to 1.5B parameter models: the 1.5B model went from 3.124 to 2.977 validation loss against the best batch-512 run. https://huggingface.co/papers/2610.15965 . Read 2026-11-11, page partly read; single preprint, no code released.
maturity: One preprint; not replicated; 4 upvotes in the sweep (no adoption signal).
cost: May not transfer to other data or model sizes; smaller batches lower throughput.
simpler_alternative: Let the hyperparameter search include batch size.
reason: Worth one dated line in a reference file as a hypothesis to test, not a rule.
cheap_local_trial: Train a model of about 30M parameters on a small repeated corpus at batch 32, 64 and 256 with equal tokens and 3 seeds each; compare validation loss. About an hour on the 32 GB GPU, not minutes.

what: Fixing three pipeline errors (loss computed over the wrong scope, shape misalignment before truncation, augmentations) improved a small forecaster's error by 43.8% with no model change.
problem_here: Supports auditing the data and loss pipeline before tuning; the kit's phased procedure is where such a step would sit.
mechanism: Code review of loss scope and tensor alignment.
evidence: Authors' own result, single seed, fixes not isolated: MASE 3.030 to 1.704. https://huggingface.co/papers/2609.31669 . Read 2026-11-11.
maturity: v0.5 preprint; repository Apache-2.0; 3 upvotes (weak signal).
cost: none beyond reading.
simpler_alternative: Whatever sanity checks the kit's procedure already has (not inspected here).
reason: An anecdote that agrees with common practice; too weak to change the procedure.
cheap_local_trial: none

what: Split mid-training compute across several independent branches and merge selected checkpoints.
problem_here: none found for a single-GPU user; it multiplies storage and validation cost.
mechanism: Branch, train, select by validation loss, average weights.
evidence: Authors' measurement: 68.96 against 68.55 for merging along one trajectory; storage and validation cost not counted. https://huggingface.co/papers/2609.37169 . Read 2026-11-11, page partly read.
maturity: Preprint; no code; 1 upvote.
cost: Several times the compute and disk for a gain of about 0.4 points.
simpler_alternative: Average the last few checkpoints of one run.
reason: Small self-reported gain at high cost; revisit if replicated.

what: The evaluator is improved alongside the agent instead of staying fixed.
problem_here: Conflicts with the brief: evaluation code must not change during the loop.
mechanism: Evaluators and agents are evolved against each other and scored on held-out tasks.
evidence: Authors' preliminary result: 82.1% against 75.0% for a fixed-evaluator baseline on held-out tasks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26294 . Read 2026-11-11.
maturity: Preprint marked preliminary; no code; 28 citations in the sweep record (weak signal).
cost: An evaluator that moves cannot anchor a reported number.
simpler_alternative: A frozen evaluator with negative controls, improved only between loops by the user.
reason: Not for the training evaluator. Keep it as a reminder that a fixed evaluator can be weak, which the negative-control check addresses.
cheap_local_trial: none

what: Edits one agent skill document step by step and accepts an edit only when the score on a selection split is strictly higher; a test split is used for reporting only.
problem_here: Goal 4 and the brief's wish for a cheap measure of whether the kit helps: the skill text must work on three agents and there is no method for tuning it per agent.
mechanism: Propose an edit, run tasks, accept on strict improvement, reject ties.
evidence: Authors' measurement: average gains of 24.8 points with one terminal agent and 19.1 with another; resulting skills 379 to 1,995 tokens; 20.8 to 213.8 million training tokens; no seeds or intervals reported. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23904 . Read 2026-11-11, page partly read. 232 citations in the sweep record (weak signal).
maturity: Paper from May 2026; code link https://aka.ms/SkillOpt not opened, license not seen.
cost: Tens to hundreds of millions of agent tokens; needs a task set with a trustworthy score; the skill can overfit the task set.
simpler_alternative: Hand-edit the skill and rerun the kit's own benchmark.
reason: The strict accept gate mirrors the kit's own keep rule and the short resulting skills support the brief's short-instructions preference. Cost and missing variance data argue for assessment first.
cheap_local_trial: Without installing anything: change one paragraph of the skill, score five fixed fake-run tasks before and after on a selection split, keep the edit only on strict improvement. Minutes of wall time per step, but agent tokens cost money.

candidate: Sharded evaluation with seeds derived from the example index
what: Split an evaluation set into disjoint index slices that run in parallel on cheap GPUs; derive each example's random seed from its index so the union of shards equals the unsharded run.
problem_here: Long evaluations slow the loop; sharding across rented GPUs must not change the reported number.
mechanism: Index-sliced shards, per-example seeds, per-example result files merged by harness code.
evidence: Workshop paper (2026-11-05), authors' measurement: 200 rollouts in 37.7 minutes for 3.49 USD on eight L4 shards (4.36 GPU-hours at 0.80 USD per hour); whole study about 34 USD; five scenes that succeed before the policy acts are excluded as artifacts. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07441 . Read 2026-11-11. The abstract and a table disagree on the number of checkpoints.
maturity: One paper; the technique itself is ordinary.
cost: The evaluator and the sealed test data must be present on every shard, which widens exposure of the sealed set; the merge code is new trusted code.
simpler_alternative: Run the evaluation once on the training machine.
reason: Useful once remote runs exist and evaluation is the bottleneck. The sealed-data exposure needs a design answer first.
cheap_local_trial: Split a validation set into four index shards, run them one after another on the local GPU with index-derived seeds, assert the merged metric equals the unsharded one. Minutes.
